frequency_question: How often do structural friction, procedural hurdles, and administrative appeals successfully prevent a federal agency from completing the revocation of an established accrediting body's authority within a short statutory window?
membership_rule: Includes any federal department review resulting in a formal threat or proceeding to strip recognition from a major national accrediting agency. Excludes voluntary relinquishments or minor probationary warnings that do not involve revocation of recognition.

cases.name: Department of Education review of American Bar Association (ABA) accreditation role (historical challenges)
Department of Education review of Accrediting Council for Independent Colleges and Schools (ACICS)
Department of Education second review and termination of ACICS

coverage_note: 3 major contested national accreditor revocation battles identified since the 1990 Higher Education Act amendments.
known_gaps: Lower-profile or regional accreditor disputes that were settled quietly without public termination orders.
skeleton: Total formal federal attempts to strip major institutional accreditor recognition since 1990 vs. successful completions of revocation resulting in final termination.
multiplier: 1 successful revocation (ACICS second attempt) out of 3 major contested high-stakes review processes equals approximately 33% base rate of successful revocation, meaning structural/procedural friction prevents revocation in about 67% of cases.
validity_reason: Administrative procedures governing federal recognition of accreditors remain anchored in the Higher Education Act and federal regulations, which change slowly.
